1994 Jan 1. DMS|RGG; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution
note: There was no date on the original document so 1994 Jan 1 was assigned since most of the SLHs were prepared from 1994 thru 1997.

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Rainwater Killifish
Scientific Name: Lucania parva

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Osteichthyes
	Order: Atheriniformes
	Family: Cyprinodontidae

nodes.title: Other Common Names
nodes.body:
Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Baird and Girard 1855)
	Reference for Classification (Robins et al.1991)
	Revision date should be checked

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial: There is no commercial value for this species.
Recreational:  Lucania has limited value as an aquarium fish (Hoedeman 1974)..
Ecological: Due to its regional abundance  Lucania is a an important part of the food chain as a predator on mosquito larvae and crustaceans and as a forage source for piscine and avian predators.
Indicator: Lack of vegetation.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  A temperate species recorded from Cape Cod, Massachusetts to Tampico, Mexico (Duggins 1983; Hoese and Moore 1977)
Within Study Area:  Found throughout the  Indian River Lagoon though most abundant at locations remote from ocean inlets and in the northern half of the Lagoon (Schooley 1980; Gilmore 1977; Gilmore 1988; Mulligan 1981; Snelson 1983; Mulligan and Snelson 1983; Brown-Peterson and Eames 1990).
Life Mode: Lucania parva is a euryoecious estuarine fish throughout its range.  It can tolerate large temperature and salinity ranges but requires  vegetated estuarine habitats for spawning.
Mobility and Migration: Adults and juveniles move in relation to hydrologic conditions.

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
Dense vegetation including mangrove prop roots, seagrass and algal communities of marine, estuarine, brackish and freshwater habitats.  Peninsular Florida - estuaries, Everglades region, coastal freshwater marshes, salt marshes, lakes, St. Johns river system and hard water springs (Dunson and Travis 1991; Duggins 1980; Loftus and Kushlan 1987; McLane 1955; Harrington and Harrington 1961; Hoese and Moore 1977; Snelson 1983; Sogard et al. 1987; Gilmore 1977)
Substrate:  Associated with substrate that will support vegetation.

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature: Temperature tolerances ranged from 6-39 C (Kilby 1955; Dunson and Travis 1991; Schooley 1980).
Salinity: Optimum salinity range 10 -15 ppt.  Salinity tolerances 0-80 ppt (Dunson and Travis 1991).  Hardy (1978) reported a salinity range from 0-48 ppt. Sogard (1987) collected large numbers in Florida Bay with salinity ranges from 17- 44 ppt.

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Gonochoristic, oviparous, polygamous, iteroparous (Parenti 1980; Hardy 1978; McLane 1955).
Mating/Spawning: Spawning involves male courtship displays and usually takes place around aquatic vegetation.  Spawning in northern part of range takes place from mid-spring to mid-summer, in the southern range spawning starts late winter and continues till late summer with peaks in early summer. In Florida spawning has been documented from February through October with the belief that it may occur all year.  Females can produce multiple broods in a year (Hardy 1978).  Schooley found peaks in the summer.
Fecundity: Rainwater killifish may produce 7-46 ova are produced per spawning event, with a mean of 24.5 during a spawning event (Hardy 1978).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg: Demersal which are either deposited on vegetation near the surface or on the bottom in shallow water. Eggs are 1.0-1.3 mm in diameter with attachment filaments covering one area of the chorion.  Incubation period is 7-14 d with 23.9 C optimum developmental temperature (Hardy 1978).
Larvae: Larvae length at hatching ranges from 4-5 mm with yolk sac absorption taking 7 days. Larvae are benthic until yolk sac absorption  (Hardy 1978).
Juvenile:  Hardy described juveniles minimum size as 20 mm TL or 42 days after hatching and exhibit the pigmentation pattern of the adults (Hardy 1978).
Adult: Adults >25 mm SL maximum length 62.5 mm with females larger than males (Hardy 1978)

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Harrington and Harrington described Lucania as mostly a carnivorous fish eating mainly mosquito larvae and copepods (1961).  McLane (1955) found larval insect parts, crustaceans and filamentous algae in the stomach contents of St. Johns River populations.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Due to its localized abundance  Lucania is an important part of the food chain as a predator on mosquito larvae and crustaceans and as a forage source for piscine and avian predators.
